front: The vasopressin chart shows it is dosed at _______ units/min as a FIXED dose — it is NOT _______. Its V1 receptor causes _______ in skin, muscle, and splanchnic vessels. The VASST trial showed _______ vs norepinephrine alone in septic shock. The maximum dose limit is _______ units/min to avoid _______.
back:
Vasopressin dosing: 0.03–0.04 units/min IV — fixed rate, NOT titrated
| Role: add-on to norepinephrine for catecholamine-sparing (when NE ≥ 20–25 mcg/min)
| V1 receptors (vascular): vasoconstriction — skin, skeletal muscle, splanchnic vasculature
| V2 receptors (renal): antidiuretic hormone effect on collecting duct
| VASST trial: vasopressin + NE vs NE alone → NO overall 90-day mortality benefit
  Subgroup benefit: less severe septic shock (NE < 15 mcg/min at baseline)
| Max dose: 0.04 units/min — higher doses risk splanchnic/digital ischemia
→ CCRN KEY: Why is vasopressin not titrated? At doses > 0.04 u/min: splanchnic ischemia (gut, liver), digital ischemia, profound hyponatremia (V2 effect on renal water reabsorption). Vasopressin is used for catecholamine-sparing — to allow NE dose reduction, reducing adrenergic side effects (arrhythmia, ischemia, metabolic effects).
→ MASTERY NOTE: ATHOS-3 trial — angiotensin II (Giapreza):
• New vasopressor for catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock
• Dose: 20 ng/kg/min to 40 ng/kg/min IV (different units from vasopressin!)
• Mechanism: RAAS activation → AT1 receptor → vasoconstriction
• FDA approved 2017 for high-output distributive shock
• Monitor: DVT risk (venous thromboembolism prophylaxis required).

front: The terlipressin chart shows it is used for _______ syndrome (HRS-AKI). The CONFIRM trial showed HRS reversal in _______ vs _______% with placebo. Terlipressin was FDA approved in _______. Its key contraindications include _______, and the nursing monitoring priority is _______.
back:
Terlipressin indication: Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS-AKI) in decompensated cirrhosis
| CONFIRM trial (NEJM 2021, n=300): terlipressin + albumin vs placebo + albumin
| HRS reversal: 32.4% vs 16.5% (SCr ≤ 1.5 mg/dL × 48h without death or dialysis)
| FDA approved: August 2022 (first FDA-approved therapy for HRS-AKI in USA)
| Dose: 1 mg IV q4–6h; ↑ to 2 mg q4–6h if SCr not ↓ ≥ 25% within 48h
| Duration: up to 14 days or until SCr < 1.5 mg/dL
| Contraindications: ischemic heart disease, severe COPD, peripheral vascular disease
| Monitoring priority: respiratory status (albumin + terlipressin → fluid retention → pulm edema)
→ CCRN KEY: HRS-AKI pathophysiology: cirrhosis → portal hypertension → splanchnic vasodilation → RAAS/SNS activation → renal vasoconstriction → functional AKI (no structural kidney damage). Diagnosis: SCr rise ≥ 0.3 mg/dL in 48h OR ≥ 50% from baseline in 7 days, in cirrhosis with ascites, no shock, no nephrotoxins, no AKI improvement after 48h IVF. Terlipressin V1 effect: splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↑ effective blood volume → ↑ renal perfusion.
→ MASTERY NOTE: Alternative HRS-AKI therapy (if terlipressin unavailable/CI):
• Midodrine 12.5 mg PO TID + octreotide 200 mcg SQ TID + albumin 1 g/kg/day × 2 then 20–40 g/day
• Less effective than terlipressin (HRS reversal ~20–30% in observational data)
• Norepinephrine IV + albumin: ICU alternative; requires vasopressor-capable monitoring
Liver transplantation remains definitive treatment — terlipressin is a bridge therapy.

front: On the vasopressin/methylene blue chart, methylene blue treats _______ syndrome by inhibiting _______ and _______, reducing cGMP and increasing _______. Dose is _______ mg/kg IV. The critical nursing monitoring pitfall is _______, and the absolute contraindication is _______.
back:
Methylene blue indication: vasoplegic syndrome (distributive shock refractory to vasopressors)
| Classic settings: post-cardiac surgery (cardiopulmonary bypass), severe anaphylaxis, drug-induced
| Mechanism: inhibits NOS (↓ NO production) AND inhibits guanylate cyclase (↓ cGMP)
| → ↓ cGMP → vascular smooth muscle contraction → ↑ SVR
| Dose: 1–2 mg/kg IV over 15–60 min; may repeat q4–6h; infusion 0.25–2 mg/kg/hr
| Absolute CI: G6PD deficiency — oxidative hemolysis
| Nursing monitoring PITFALL: pulse oximetry falsely reads LOW (blue dye absorbs at 668 nm)
→ CCRN KEY: Vasoplegic syndrome after cardiac surgery:
Mechanism: CPB → complement activation + endotoxin exposure + hypothermia → massive NO release → profound SVR drop (CI normal or ↑, MAP < 65 despite high-dose NE). Management: NE first-line + vasopressin → if refractory → methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV bolus. Response: ↑ SVR within 1–2h, ↓ vasopressor requirements in 60–70% of cases.
→ MASTERY NOTE: Methylene blue pulse ox interference — clinical management:
• SpO₂ may read 65–70% despite true normal saturation during infusion
• Use ABG for accurate SaO₂ measurement during methylene blue infusion
• Effect lasts 30–60 min after infusion ends as dye is metabolized/excreted
Serotonin syndrome risk: methylene blue inhibits MAO-A → excess serotonin with SSRIs/MAOIs. Expected harmless effects: urine blue-green, skin/mucosa appear cyanotic (dye) — document at medication start to prevent alarm calls from nursing staff change of shift. Hydroxocobalamin (cyanide antidote) also treats vasoplegic via NO scavenging — alternative.

front: On the antidote chart, opioid toxicity is reversed with _______ at _______ mg IV every 2–3 minutes. Because its half-life is only _______ minutes, a continuous infusion of _______ of the effective reversal dose per hour is often needed to prevent _______.
back:
Naloxone (Narcan) — opioid reversal
| Dose: 0.4–2 mg IV every 2–3 minutes, titrated to RR > 12/min (not full reversal)
| Half-life: 30–90 minutes (shorter than most opioids, especially extended-release)
| Infusion: 2/3 of the effective reversal dose per hour (prevents re-narcotization)
| Goal: adequate respiratory rate — NOT full reversal (precipitates withdrawal)
→ CCRN KEY: Opioid-induced respiratory depression = RR < 12, pinpoint pupils, decreased LOC. Naloxone in opioid-dependent patients: start with 0.04–0.1 mg titrated doses to avoid acute withdrawal (seizures, vomiting, hypertensive crisis, dysrhythmia). Re-narcotization risk is highest with long-acting agents: methadone (t½ 24–36h), oxycodone ER, fentanyl patches — monitor for 4–12h after reversal.
→ MASTERY NOTE: After effective reversal, calculate naloxone infusion as 2/3 of the total dose needed to achieve reversal, given hourly (e.g., if 2 mg reversed the patient, infuse 1.3 mg/hr). Observe for at least 2× the expected opioid duration. Naloxone also available IM/intranasal (Narcan nasal spray 4 mg) — ICU uses IV route. Subcutaneous or SQ routes slower onset — use only if IV access unavailable.

front: The pulmonary vasodilators chart shows inhaled NO works by entering pulmonary vascular SMCs and increasing _______, causing selective pulmonary vasodilation without _______. Dose range is _______ ppm. A critical monitoring parameter is _______ (check every 4–8 hours), and abrupt discontinuation causes _______.
back:
Inhaled NO (iNO) mechanism: diffuses into pulmonary vascular SMC → activates guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP → vasodilation
| Selective: inactivated by Hgb before reaching systemic circulation — no systemic hypotension
| Dose: 1–40 ppm (start 10–20 ppm; titrate to SpO₂/PaO₂ response)
| Methemoglobin: NO + Hgb → metHgb; check q4–8h; stop if > 5%
| Abrupt discontinuation → rebound pulmonary hypertension (wean gradually over hours)
→ CCRN KEY: iNO indication — refractory hypoxemia in ARDS (P/F < 100 despite LPV + PEEP), RV failure with pulmonary hypertension, post-cardiac surgery PH crisis. iNO improves V/Q matching (selectively vasodilates ventilated alveolar units). Multiple RCTs (ARDS): NO survival benefit — temporary oxygenation improvement only. Use as bridge to ECMO or to allow time for LPV to work.
→ MASTERY NOTE: Second monitoring parameter: NO₂ (nitrogen dioxide) — toxic byproduct when iNO reacts with O₂ in the ventilator circuit. Monitor with inline NO₂ detector; levels should be < 3 ppm. Cost: iNO is extremely expensive ($3,000–10,000/day). Inhaled epoprostenol = cost-effective alternative with equivalent effect and less monitoring burden. Methemoglobin > 5%: stop iNO; give methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg if symptomatic metHgb.

front: On the thrombolytics chart, massive PE is defined as acute PE plus _______. The standard alteplase dose is _______ mg IV over _______ hours. Heparin should be _______ during infusion and restarted WITHOUT a bolus when aPTT < _______.
back:
Massive PE definition: acute PE + hemodynamic instability
| SBP < 90 mmHg OR vasopressor-dependent OR cardiac arrest
| Alteplase standard dose: 100 mg IV over 2 hours
| Heparin: HOLD during alteplase infusion; restart WITHOUT bolus when aPTT < 80
→ CCRN KEY: Indication for systemic thrombolysis = massive PE (hemodynamically unstable). Do NOT give systemic lysis for submassive PE (intermediate-risk) unless imminent decompensation — bleeding risk (ICH ~2%) outweighs benefit in stable patients (PEITHO trial). Assessment after lysis: repeat echo at 2h — expect ↓ RV dilation, ↑ BP, ↑ SpO₂.
→ MASTERY NOTE: Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT):
• Dose: 10–20 mg alteplase over 6–24h via pulmonary artery catheter
• Advantage: lower dose → lower bleeding risk vs systemic; preferred for submassive PE
• Requires: interventional radiology suite; specialized catheter placement
VA-ECMO for massive PE with refractory cardiac arrest:
• Bridge to percutaneous thrombectomy or surgical embolectomy
• Can also allow thrombolytics to work while maintaining cardiac output on ECMO
Surgical embolectomy: consider when lysis fails or is absolutely contraindicated + surgical expertise and operating room immediately available.

front: On the antidote chart, organophosphate toxicity requires _______ (titrated to _______, not heart rate) PLUS _______ to reactivate acetylcholinesterase. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) must be given _______ to be effective.
back:
Organophosphate toxicity → Atropine + Pralidoxime (2-PAM):
| Atropine: 2–4 mg IV every 5–10 min; titrate to DRY secretions (not HR or pupil size)
| 2-PAM: 1–2 g IV; must give EARLY — AChE 'aging' becomes irreversible at 24–48h
| Toxidrome (SLUDGE): Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis
| Also: bradycardia, miosis, bronchospasm (muscarinic excess)
→ CCRN KEY: Atropine endpoint = DRY secretions + clear lung sounds — NOT HR or pupil size. Doses up to 20–100 mg may be needed in severe poisoning. 2-PAM prevents new ACh binding but cannot reverse 'aged' (covalently bound) AChE.
→ MASTERY NOTE: Pralidoxime window: give within 24–48h before irreversible AChE aging. After aging: atropine controls symptoms; 2-PAM no longer reactivates. Sources: pesticides (malathion, parathion), nerve agents (sarin, VX).

front: The APROCCHSS trial (NEJM 2018) added _______ mcg/day of _______ to hydrocortisone 200 mg/day and DID show mortality benefit (_______ vs _______%). The SSC trigger for steroids in septic shock is NE or Epi ≥ _______ mcg/kg/min.
back:
APROCCHSS (NEJM 2018, n=1,241): hydrocortisone 200 mg/day + fludrocortisone 50 mcg/day × 7 days
| MORTALITY BENEFIT: 43.0% vs 49.1% at 90 days (p=0.03)
| Key difference from ADRENAL: fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid) added
| SSC trigger: NE or Epi ≥ 0.25 mcg/kg/min despite adequate fluid resuscitation
→ CCRN KEY: APROCCHSS vs ADRENAL — why different results?
APROCCHSS added fludrocortisone 50 mcg/day PO. Whether fludrocortisone explains the mortality difference remains debated — different patient populations also differed.
→ MASTERY NOTE: Fludrocortisone: mineralocorticoid receptor agonist → Na/water retention, K excretion. At hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (inherent mineralocorticoid effect), additional fludrocortisone may be redundant — hence the ongoing controversy.

front: On the receptor map chart, α1 receptors are located on _______ smooth muscle cells and cause _______. Pure α1 agonist _______ causes a reflex _______ because it has no _______ activity. β2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle cause _______, and β2 stimulation also shifts potassium _______.
back:
α1 receptors: vascular SMC → vasoconstriction, ↑ SVR
| Pure α1 agonist: phenylephrine — causes reflex bradycardia (baroreceptor response to ↑ BP)
| Reflex bradycardia: because phenylephrine has NO β1 activity (NE has β1 → no reflex)
| β2 receptors: bronchial SMC → bronchodilation; also peripheral vasodilation, ↓ SVR
| β2 stimulation: shifts K⁺ INTO cells (intracellular) → hypokalemia
→ CCRN KEY: Receptor profiles of common vasopressors:
• Norepinephrine: α1 >> β1 > β2 — vasopressor with mild inotropy; minimal ↓ SVR
• Epinephrine: α1 + β1 + β2 — all doses; low dose: β2 dominates (↑ CO, ↓ SVR)
• Dopamine dose-dependent: 1–3 = DA; 5–10 = β1; > 10 = α1 (but variable, not precise)
• Dobutamine: β1 + β2 (weak α1) — ↑ CO + modest ↓ SVR; cardiogenic shock
→ MASTERY NOTE: Phenylephrine clinical niche:
Vasodilatory shock with PRESERVED or HIGH cardiac output (septic shock with adequate CO + low SVR). Advantage: pure vasoconstriction without chronotropy — useful in AF with rapid ventricular rate when NE would further increase HR. AVOID in cardiogenic shock (↑ afterload → ↑ myocardial O₂ demand). Also used: nasal decongestant, pupil dilation, spinal anesthesia hypotension.

front: The receptor chart shows dopamine receptors (DA1) cause renal _______, and 'renal dose dopamine' (1–3 mcg/kg/min) is _______ recommended by evidence. Muscarinic (mAChR) blockade by _______ treats organophosphate toxicity by drying secretions. The muscarinic M2 receptor at the SA node mediates _______ when stimulated.
back:
DA1 receptors: renal and mesenteric vasodilation → ↑ GFR + natriuresis
| Renal dose dopamine (1–3 mcg/kg/min): NOT recommended — no evidence prevents AKI or reduces mortality
| Fenoldopam (selective DA1 agonist): used for hypertensive crisis (↑ renal blood flow + ↓ BP)
| mAChR (muscarinic) blockade by atropine: dries secretions, ↑ HR, reverses bronchospasm
| M2 receptor at SA/AV nodes: vagal stimulation → ↓ HR, ↓ AV conduction (vasovagal response)
→ CCRN KEY: Why is 'renal dose dopamine' no longer used?
• Bellomo trial (NEJM 2000, n=328): low-dose dopamine vs placebo in ICU — NO difference in peak Cr, RRT requirement, or mortality.
• Risk: tachyarrhythmias even at 'low' doses; variable receptor activation at same dose
• Alternative: optimize volume status, avoid nephrotoxins, treat hypotension with appropriate vasopressors
→ MASTERY NOTE: Atropine receptor pharmacology in clinical practice:
• Atropine: non-selective mAChR blocker (M1/M2/M3)
• M2 blockade → ↑ HR (blocks vagal tone) — use: bradycardia, organophosphate, succinylcholine bradycardia in children
• M3 blockade → ↓ secretions, bronchodilation, ↑ pupil (mydriasis)
• High-dose atropine in organophosphate poisoning: endpoint is DRY SECRETIONS (M3 effect), not heart rate — tachycardia is expected and acceptable during treatment.

front: On the coagulation reversal chart, warfarin reversal for INR > 6 with life-threatening bleeding uses _______ units/kg of 4F-PCC PLUS _______. Protamine reverses UFH at _______ mg per _______ units of heparin. Tranexamic acid (TXA) is given in trauma within _______ hours and works by inhibiting _______.
back:
Warfarin reversal — life-threatening bleeding:
| 4F-PCC (KCentra) dose: INR > 6 → 50 units/kg IV (max 5,000 units)
| Must also give Vitamin K 10 mg IV (prevents re-elevation when PCC factors wear off at 6–12h)
| Protamine: 1 mg per 100 units UFH; max 50 mg per dose
  Partially reverses LMWH (~60%): give if recent LMWH; does NOT reverse fondaparinux
| TXA (tranexamic acid): inhibits plasminogen → prevents fibrinolysis → stabilizes clot
| Trauma: give within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2 trial: ↓ mortality; harmful if > 3h delay)
→ CCRN KEY: 4F-PCC vs FFP for warfarin reversal:
• 4F-PCC: immediate reversal, small volume (25–50 mL vs liters of FFP), no thaw time
• FFP: reverses all factors but requires 15–20 min thaw, 10–15 mL/kg volume → fluid overload risk
• 4F-PCC preferred for: urgent reversal, heart failure, volume-sensitive patients
→ MASTERY NOTE: TXA clinical applications beyond trauma:
• OB hemorrhage: 1 g IV within 3h of delivery (WHO/WOMAN trial — ↓ mortality from PPH)
• Cardiac surgery: perioperative TXA → ↓ transfusion requirements (ATACAS trial)
• Intracerebral hemorrhage: TICH-2 trial — TXA did NOT improve outcomes at 90 days (no benefit)
• Topical: oral rinse for gingival bleeding in anticoagulated patients; ophthalmic surgery
TXA adverse effects: venous thromboembolism (monitor), seizures at high doses (GABA antagonism).

front: On the renal dose adjustment chart, morphine is problematic in AKI because its active metabolite _______ accumulates, causing _______. The preferred opioid in AKI/CKD is _______. In CrCl < 30 mL/min, LMWH (enoxaparin) should be _______ and replaced with _______ monitored by _______.
back:
Morphine in AKI: active metabolite M6G (morphine-6-glucuronide) accumulates → respiratory depression
| Preferred opioid in AKI: hydromorphone (no active accumulating metabolites in moderate CKD)
| Fentanyl: safe in CKD (hepatic metabolism, extrahepatic clearance) — preferred in severe AKI
| LMWH (enoxaparin) in CrCl < 30: AVOID therapeutic dose (anti-Xa accumulation → bleeding)
| Replace with: UFH (unfractionated heparin) — not renally cleared; monitor aPTT or anti-Xa
| UFH monitoring: aPTT 60–100s or anti-Xa 0.3–0.7 IU/mL
→ CCRN KEY: Opioid metabolism in renal failure — summary:
• Codeine: avoid in AKI — accumulation of active metabolites; CYP2D6 variability too
• Tramadol: avoid in CrCl < 30 — active metabolites accumulate → seizure risk
• Meperidine: AVOID in CKD — normeperidine accumulates → tremors, myoclonus, seizures
• Hydromorphone: can be used with dose reduction in moderate CKD; avoid in ESRD
• Fentanyl: preferred in ESRD/dialysis patients (hepatic/extrahepatic clearance)
→ MASTERY NOTE: Gabapentin/pregabalin in CKD:
• 100% renally cleared — significant accumulation in CKD
• Normal dose: gabapentin 300 mg TID → in CrCl 15–29: 200–700 mg/day (single daily dose)
• Clinical effect of accumulation: somnolence, respiratory depression, fall risk
• Dialysis patients: gabapentin 100–300 mg after each dialysis session (removed by HD).

front: The antibiotic mechanisms chart shows beta-lactams inhibit _______ (PBPs), blocking _______. Cefepime (4th generation) covers gram-negatives including _______. Vancomycin instead inhibits _______ and is monitored by _______ target of _______.
back:
Beta-lactams inhibit PBPs (penicillin-binding proteins = transpeptidases) → block cell wall cross-linking
| Cefepime (4th generation): gram-positive + Pseudomonas aeruginosa + some ESBL (not reliable)
| Ceftaroline (5th generation): MRSA-active cephalosporin
| Carbapenems (meropenem/imipenem): broadest coverage including ESBL — NOT MRSA
| Vancomycin: inhibits cell wall transglycosylation (different from PBP inhibition)
| Vancomycin monitoring: AUC/MIC target 400–600 (PK/PD-guided, not just trough)
→ CCRN KEY: Beta-lactam resistance mechanisms:
• MRSA: altered PBP (PBP2a) — methicillin/oxacillin resistance; all beta-lactams EXCEPT ceftaroline fail
• ESBL (extended-spectrum beta-lactamase): hydrolysis of penicillins + cephalosporins; carbapenems active
• Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE/KPC): carbapenemase enzymes — use ceftazidime-avibactam
→ MASTERY NOTE: Pip-tazobactam (4.5g q6h extended 4-hour infusion) vs standard 30-min infusion:
• Beta-lactam killing = TIME above MIC (not peak concentration)
• Extended infusion: 4h drip maintains drug concentration above Pseudomonas MIC for 50% of dosing interval
• Standard bolus: same dose but rapid clearance → drug level drops below MIC too quickly
• Clinical outcome: extended infusion associated with ↓ mortality in P. aeruginosa bacteremia (retrospective).

front: The antibiotic chart shows aminoglycosides inhibit the _______ ribosomal subunit. The preferred dosing strategy is _______ (once-daily) because aminoglycosides show _______ dependent killing. Linezolid covers _______ and _______, but causes _______ syndrome risk when combined with serotonergic drugs.
back:
Aminoglycosides: inhibit 30S ribosomal subunit → misreading of mRNA → aberrant protein synthesis
| Preferred dosing: once-daily (extended interval) — concentration-dependent killing
| Goal: high peak/MIC ratio (Cmax/MIC > 8–10) achieved by larger single dose
| Nephrotoxicity: proximal tubule accumulation — less with once-daily than multiple daily doses
| Linezolid (oxazolidinone): inhibits 50S + 30S — unique mechanism; bacteriostatic
| Coverage: MRSA + VRE (FDA-approved); also resistant gram+ when vancomycin fails
| Serotonin syndrome risk: MAO-A inhibition → avoid with SSRIs, MAOIs, tramadol
→ CCRN KEY: Aminoglycoside toxicity monitoring:
• Nephrotoxicity: ↑ SCr, tubular casts; risk ↑ with: hypovolemia, other nephrotoxins, prolonged course
• Ototoxicity: irreversible (cochlear + vestibular); risk ↑ with total cumulative dose
• Traditional monitoring: trough < 1 mcg/mL (gentamicin/tobramycin); peak 8–10 mcg/mL
• AUC-guided monitoring increasingly used for vancomycin AND aminoglycosides
→ MASTERY NOTE: Daptomycin — cell membrane disruption (gram-positive only):
• Approved: MRSA bacteremia, endocarditis, SSTI
• Do NOT use for pneumonia — inactivated by pulmonary surfactant
• Monitor: CK levels (myopathy — check weekly); hold statins if CK ↑
• Tigecycline (50S inhibitor): broad spectrum (MRSA + ESBL + anaerobes) — but ↑ mortality in VAP trial; use only when no alternatives for non-lung infections.

front: The CYP2C19 chart shows clopidogrel is a _______ requiring CYP2C19 activation. PPIs inhibit CYP2C19 — the safest PPI to use with clopidogrel is _______ because it is the weakest CYP2C19 inhibitor. Patients who are CYP2D6 poor metabolizers cannot effectively convert _______ to morphine, resulting in _______.
back:
Clopidogrel: prodrug — must be activated by CYP2C19 to active thiol metabolite
| PPIs inhibit CYP2C19 → ↓ clopidogrel activation → ↓ platelet inhibition
| Safest PPI with clopidogrel: pantoprazole (weakest CYP2C19 inhibitor)
| Avoid: omeprazole (strongest 2C19 inhibitor — most clinical concern with clopidogrel)
| CYP2D6 poor metabolizers (PM): cannot convert codeine → morphine (no analgesic effect)
| CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolizers (UM): excessive morphine conversion → respiratory depression
→ CCRN KEY: Clinical implications of clopidogrel-PPI interaction:
• FDA warning (2009): avoid omeprazole + clopidogrel concurrently
• Clinical evidence: COGENT trial — omeprazole + clopidogrel: no ↑ CV events (underpowered)
• Current practice: use pantoprazole if GI protection needed with clopidogrel-based therapy
→ MASTERY NOTE: Pharmacogenomics in ICU pain management:
• CPIC guidelines: do not use codeine in CYP2D6 UM or PM patients
• Tramadol: 2D6-metabolized; PM = no effect; UM = toxicity; avoid when status unknown
• Metoprolol: 2D6 substrate; fluoxetine/paroxetine (2D6 inhibitors) → ↑ metoprolol → bradycardia
• Routine pharmacogenomic testing increasingly available — relevant for long-term ICU pain management.

front: The coagulation chart shows the extrinsic pathway is measured by _______ (INR) and the intrinsic pathway by _______. UFH works by binding _______, which then inhibits factors _______ and _______.
back:
Extrinsic pathway (PT/INR): tissue factor + factor VII → activates factor X
| Intrinsic pathway (aPTT): XII → XI → IX → X (with factor VIII as cofactor)
| UFH mechanism: binds antithrombin (AT) → AT-UFH complex inhibits IIa (thrombin) + Xa
→ CCRN KEY: UFH monitoring options:
• aPTT: most widely used; target 60–100s (therapeutic)
• Anti-Xa: target 0.3–0.7 IU/mL; preferred in obesity, APS, abnormal baseline aPTT
• ACT (activated clotting time): cardiac cath lab/bypass; target > 300s for CPB
→ MASTERY NOTE: Why aPTT measures intrinsic pathway: uses a contact activator (kaolin, silica) to start at factor XII. PT/INR uses tissue factor to start at factor VII. Both converge at factor X (common pathway).

front: On the sedation comparison chart, propofol works by _______ and has a unique toxicity at doses > _______ mg/kg/hr for > 48 hours called _______ syndrome, which presents with _______, rhabdomyolysis, and _______. Propofol has _______ analgesic effect.
back:
Propofol mechanism: potentiates GABA-A receptor (allosteric modulation)
| PRIS (Propofol Infusion Syndrome): doses > 4 mg/kg/hr for > 48 hours
| PRIS presentation: lactic acidosis + rhabdomyolysis + AV conduction block + lipemic plasma
| NO analgesic effect — always combine with opioid or other analgesic
| Propofol 1%: 0.1 g fat (10 kcal) per mL → monitor triglycerides weekly
→ CCRN KEY: PRIS recognition in ICU:
• Risk factors: high doses, prolonged use, children, low carbohydrate intake, catecholamine/steroid use
• Early signs: metabolic acidosis (elevated anion gap), rising lactate, ↑ CK
• Late signs: cardiac arrhythmia (AV block, Brugada-like pattern on ECG), renal failure
• Action: STOP propofol immediately; switch to alternative sedation; supportive care ± CVVH
→ MASTERY NOTE: Propofol vs dexmedetomidine for ICU sedation (key differences):
• Propofol: faster onset/offset; no respiratory depression at low doses (< 50 mcg/kg/min)
  BUT: no analgesia, hypotension/bradycardia, PRIS risk, hypertriglyceridemia
• Dexmedetomidine: cooperative sedation (patient arousable), analgesic, no GABA mechanism
  BUT: slower onset, bradycardia from loading dose, more expensive
• PAD guidelines prefer dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines for ICU sedation (↓ delirium).

front: On the sedation chart, dexmedetomidine is unique because it provides sedation WITHOUT _______ depression. It acts on _______ receptors in the _______. Ketamine provides sedation AND analgesia via _______ receptor antagonism and is preferred for intubation in _______ because it is a _______ agent. Ketamine also causes _______ making it useful in asthma.
back:
Dexmedetomidine: sedation WITHOUT respiratory depression (unique among ICU sedatives)
| Mechanism: α2-adrenergic receptors in locus coeruleus (brainstem) → ↓ NE release → sedation
| Clinical: cooperative ('arousable') sedation — patient responds to voice, follows commands
| Ketamine: NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor antagonist → dissociative analgesia/anesthesia
| Preferred for intubation in hemodynamic instability (hemorrhagic shock, trauma, sepsis)
| Sympathomimetic: ketamine ↑ HR, ↑ BP (endogenous catecholamine release) — safe in shock
| Bronchodilation: via β2 stimulation + direct smooth muscle relaxation → use in asthma RSI
→ CCRN KEY: Ketamine RSI (rapid sequence intubation) indications:
• Hemodynamic instability: safest induction agent (↑ BP vs ↓ with propofol/etomidate)
• Status asthmaticus requiring intubation: bronchodilator + induction agent
• Ketamine dose: 1–2 mg/kg IV (induction) or 0.1–0.5 mg/kg/hr (ICU analgesic/sedation adjunct)
• Co-administer midazolam 0.05–0.1 mg/kg to prevent emergence phenomena (hallucinations)
→ MASTERY NOTE: Ketamine and ICP — the controversy:
• Old teaching: ketamine raises ICP (avoid in TBI) — based on spontaneously breathing patients
• Modern evidence: mechanically ventilated patients with controlled ventilation → ICP does NOT rise
• Current practice: ketamine is acceptable for RSI in TBI patients — no absolute contraindication
Ketamine analgesic use: 0.1–0.3 mg/kg/hr IV → opioid-sparing; useful in opioid-tolerant patients.

front: The sedation chart shows midazolam is associated with _______ in ICU compared to propofol and dexmedetomidine. In hepatic failure, the preferred benzodiazepine is _______ because it undergoes _______ without producing active metabolites. Lorazepam IV infusions can cause toxicity from the carrier _______, presenting as _______ gap and metabolic _______.
back:
Midazolam in ICU: associated with ↑ delirium vs propofol and dexmedetomidine (MIDEX/MENDS trials)
| Accumulates with prolonged infusion (active metabolite α-hydroxymidazolam in AKI)
| Indicated for: seizures (first-line IV benzo for status epilepticus), alcohol withdrawal, procedural sedation
| Hepatic failure preferred benzo: lorazepam (direct glucuronidation — no CYP450, no active metabolites)
| Lorazepam IV carrier: propylene glycol (PG) — osmotically active
| PG toxicity: elevated osmol gap + anion gap metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis from PG itself)
→ CCRN KEY: Identifying propylene glycol toxicity in ICU:
• Patient on continuous lorazepam infusion > 3 days OR high-dose requirements
• Labs: ↑ osmol gap (osmol gap = measured − calculated osmolality; normal < 10)
• Progression: metabolic acidosis (PG metabolized to lactic acid and pyruvate)
• Management: switch to non-PG formulation OR alternative sedative
→ MASTERY NOTE: Benzodiazepine selection in ICU — hierarchy:
• Short-term procedural/seizure: midazolam (fastest onset, shortest duration)
• Alcohol withdrawal (CIWA-Ar protocol): lorazepam or diazepam — titrated to CIWA score
• Hepatic failure + ongoing sedation: lorazepam (no active metabolites via direct conjugation)
• Avoid diazepam: very long t½ (20–100h) + active metabolite desmethyldiazepam → prolonged sedation
PAD guidelines (2018): minimize benzos in ICU; prefer propofol or dexmedetomidine for light sedation.

front: The antifungal selection chart shows mucormycosis requires _______ amphotericin B PLUS surgical _______. Cryptococcus meningitis is treated with _______ PLUS _______ for induction × _______ weeks, then _______ for consolidation. The key difference between conventional and liposomal amphotericin B is _______.
back:
Mucormycosis treatment: liposomal amphotericin B 3–5 mg/kg/day PLUS surgical debridement (essential)
| Azoles (including voriconazole) and echinocandins: NOT active against Mucorales
| Isavuconazole: some activity against Mucor — salvage therapy when AmB not tolerated
Cryptococcus meningitis (HIV/immunocompromised):
| Induction (2 weeks): liposomal amphotericin B 3–4 mg/kg/day + flucytosine 25 mg/kg PO q6h
| Consolidation (8 weeks): fluconazole 400 mg/day
| Maintenance (HIV, CD4 > 200 × 3 months): fluconazole 200 mg/day
| Conventional vs liposomal AmB: liposomal has ↓ nephrotoxicity + ↓ infusion reactions — preferred in ICU
→ CCRN KEY: Amphotericin B monitoring in ICU:
• BMP daily (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Cr): AmB causes dose-dependent nephrotoxicity + electrolyte wasting
• Hypokalemia: treat aggressively (IV KCl) — often requires 100–200 mEq/day replacement
• Hypomagnesemia: concurrent — replacement required (potassium hard to correct without Mg normalization)
• Infusion-related reactions (conventional AmB): rigors, fever, hypotension — premedicate with acetaminophen
→ MASTERY NOTE: Flucytosine (5-FC) in combination therapy:
• Mechanism: converted to 5-fluorouracil inside fungal cells → DNA/RNA synthesis inhibition
• Synergistic with AmB for Cryptococcus (standard of care — CSF sterilization at 2 weeks)
• Toxicity: bone marrow suppression (monitor CBC 2×/week), GI toxicity, hepatotoxicity
• Renally cleared: dose adjust in AKI (check 5-FC levels, target 20–80 mcg/mL at 2h post-dose)
• Do NOT use flucytosine as monotherapy: resistance develops rapidly.

front: The MRSA coverage chart shows vancomycin is monitored by _______ target of _______ (not trough alone). Daptomycin is CONTRAINDICATED for MRSA _______ because it is inactivated by _______. The ZEPHyR trial found _______ superior to vancomycin for MRSA VAP with a clinical cure rate of _______ vs _______.
back:
Vancomycin monitoring: AUC/MIC ratio target 400–600 (PK/PD-guided dosing)
| Trough-only monitoring underestimates exposure — AUC-guided preferred (2018 ASHP/SIDP guideline)
| Daptomycin contraindicated for: pneumonia (lung infections) — inactivated by pulmonary surfactant
| ZEPHyR trial (NEJM 2012): linezolid vs vancomycin for MRSA VAP
| Result: linezolid clinical cure 57.6% vs vancomycin 46.6% (P=0.042); ↑ nephrotoxicity with vancomycin
→ CCRN KEY: When to prefer linezolid over vancomycin for MRSA:
• MRSA pneumonia (VAP/HAP): linezolid achieves better lung tissue penetration than vancomycin
• Vancomycin MIC ≥ 2 mcg/mL (MIC creep): poor outcomes — switch to daptomycin (non-pulmonary) or linezolid
• VISA (vancomycin-intermediate S. aureus): vancomycin fails — use daptomycin 8–10 mg/kg + adjunct
→ MASTERY NOTE: Linezolid adverse effects requiring nursing monitoring:
1. Thrombocytopenia: platelets < 100K in ~30% of patients > 14 days — CBC weekly
2. Serotonin syndrome: MAO-A inhibitor — do NOT combine with SSRIs, MAOIs, meperidine, tramadol
3. Optic neuropathy: rare, with courses > 28 days — baseline visual acuity assessment
4. Peripheral neuropathy: long-term use > 28 days; irreversible
5. Lactic acidosis: rare; from mitochondrial toxicity (inhibits mitochondrial protein synthesis).

front: The cardiogenic shock chart shows dobutamine primarily stimulates _______ receptors, increasing cardiac output and modestly _______ SVR. Milrinone works by inhibiting _______, which is different from dobutamine. The IABP-SHOCK II trial showed IABP _______ mortality in cardiogenic shock. The hemodynamic target in cardiogenic shock is cardiac index ≥ _______ L/min/m².
back:
Dobutamine: β1 (+ β2 + weak α1) agonist → ↑ CO + modest ↓ SVR (β2 vasodilation)
| Cardiogenic shock first-line inotrope; dose 2–20 mcg/kg/min; tachycardia + arrhythmia at higher doses
| Milrinone: PDE3 (phosphodiesterase-3) inhibitor → ↑ cAMP → ↑ inotropy + lusitropy + vasodilation
| Milrinone advantage: no catecholamine receptor tolerance; renally cleared (↓ dose in CKD)
| IABP-SHOCK II (NEJM 2012, n=600): IABP vs medical therapy in AMI cardiogenic shock
| Result: NO mortality benefit from IABP (30-day mortality: 39.7% vs 41.3%)
| Cardiogenic shock CI target: ≥ 2.2 L/min/m² (PCWP target ≤ 18 mmHg)
→ CCRN KEY: Dobutamine vs milrinone for cardiogenic shock:
• Both ↑ CO and ↓ SVR — similar hemodynamic effect
• Dobutamine: more arrhythmogenic (β-receptor stimulation); tachycardia limits dosing
• Milrinone: vasodilation can worsen hypotension — often needs NE added; avoid in severe hypotension
• OPTIME-CHF trial: milrinone vs dobutamine in decompensated HF — no mortality difference
→ MASTERY NOTE: Mechanical circulatory support in cardiogenic shock:
• Impella (CP/5.5): LV mechanical support → ↑ forward flow + ↓ LV work (unloads LV)
  RECOVER trial: no mortality benefit from routine Impella in AMI-CS (vs IABP)
• VA-ECMO: complete heart + lung bypass — most support possible; for refractory arrest
  Complications: ↑ LV afterload (LV venting often needed: Impella + ECMO = ECMELLA)
• SHOCK trial (NEJM 1999): early revascularization for STEMI cardiogenic shock → ↓ 6-month mortality.

front: On the beta-blocker comparison chart, esmolol has an ultra-short half-life of _______ minutes because it is metabolized by _______. For type A aortic dissection, the target heart rate is _______ and SBP < _______ mmHg, achieved with esmolol PLUS _______. The non-selective beta-blocker required for esophageal variceal prophylaxis is _______ because it requires _______ receptor blockade.
back:
Esmolol half-life: 9 minutes — metabolized by plasma esterase (red blood cell esterase)
| No hepatic or renal dependence — safe in organ failure; easily titrated (load + infusion)
| Type A aortic dissection targets: HR < 60 bpm + SBP < 120 mmHg (then surgical repair)
| Esmolol + nicardipine OR nitroprusside: combination for dissection (β-blocker FIRST to prevent reflex tachycardia from vasodilator)
| Esophageal variceal prophylaxis: propranolol (or nadolol) — non-selective required
| Reason: β2 blockade → ↓ portal blood flow (splanchnic vasodilation reversed by β2 block)
| Metoprolol (β1 selective) does NOT reduce portal pressure — cannot substitute
→ CCRN KEY: Aortic dissection drug sequence:
1. Control HR FIRST with IV esmolol or metoprolol
2. THEN add vasodilator (nitroprusside/nicardipine) to control BP
• If vasodilator given first: reflex tachycardia → ↑ aortic shear force → propagation of dissection
→ MASTERY NOTE: Beta-blocker selectivity comparison:
• β1 selective (cardioselective): metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol
  Relative selectivity — NOT absolute: still block β2 at high doses
  Relative safety in mild-moderate COPD/asthma (vs non-selective)
• Non-selective (β1+β2): propranolol, carvedilol, labetalol, nadolol
  β2 blockade → ↑ risk of bronchospasm in asthma — avoid in severe asthma
• Alpha + beta: carvedilol (α1+β1+β2), labetalol (α1+β1+β2, 3:1 β:α)
  Additional α1 block → ↓ afterload + antioxidant effects (carvedilol in HFrEF).

front: On the beta-blocker chart, labetalol blocks _______ and _______ receptors in a _______ to _______ β:α ratio. It is first-line for hypertensive emergency in _______ (pregnancy complication). Beta-blockers are absolutely contraindicated in _______ (type of shock) and relatively contraindicated in _______ and severe bradycardia.
back:
Labetalol receptor profile: β1 + β2 + α1 blockade in 3:1 β:α ratio (oral) / 7:1 (IV)
| IV dosing: 10–20 mg IV q10–15 min (bolus) OR 2 mg/min infusion; max 300 mg
| First-line for preeclampsia/eclampsia hypertension (preferred over nitroprusside — maternal/fetal safety)
| Hydralazine: alternative for preeclampsia when labetalol unavailable
| Absolute contraindication for all beta-blockers: cardiogenic shock (↓ contractility → ↓ CO)
| Relative CI: severe asthma (bronchospasm from β2 block), severe COPD, sick sinus syndrome, AV block > 1st degree
→ CCRN KEY: Hypertensive emergency beta-blocker selection:
• Acute aortic dissection: esmolol IV (fastest titration) + vasodilator
• Preeclampsia: labetalol IV (preferred) or hydralazine IV
• Hypertensive encephalopathy/stroke: nicardipine or labetalol (clevidipine for post-cardiac surgery)
• Post-CABG hypertension: esmolol + nicardipine; rapidly reversible
→ MASTERY NOTE: Beta-blocker reversal if overdose (or adverse reaction):
• Glucagon: 5–10 mg IV bolus → 1–5 mg/hr infusion (bypasses β-receptor → ↑ cAMP directly)
• Calcium chloride: 1 g IV (improves calcium-mediated contractility, especially with CCB co-ingestion)
• Atropine: for bradycardia component (less effective in complete AV block from OD)
• High-dose insulin (HDI): 1 unit/kg/hr with dextrose — positive inotropy independent of β-receptors
• Lipid emulsion therapy: for lipophilic beta-blocker overdose (propranolol, metoprolol).

front: On the vasopressor algorithm chart, vasopressin is added at fixed dose _______ units/min when NE reaches _______ mcg/kg/min. Epinephrine as a third-line vasopressor raises _______, making _______ clearance unreliable as a resuscitation endpoint.
back:
Vasopressin: added at 0.03–0.04 units/min (fixed) when NE ≥ 0.25 mcg/kg/min
| NOT titrated — fixed dose only; max 0.04 units/min to avoid splanchnic/digital ischemia
| V1 receptors (vascular): vasoconstriction — skin, muscle, splanchnic vasculature
| Epinephrine third-line: raises serum lactate (β2 → glycogenolysis + liver lactate production)
| When epi used: lactate clearance unreliable — use ScvO₂, MAP, or clinical perfusion markers
→ CCRN KEY: Vasopressor hierarchy (SSC 2021):
1. NE | 2. Vasopressin (add-on) | 3. Epinephrine | 4. Angiotensin II (Giapreza)
→ MASTERY NOTE: VASST trial: vasopressin + NE vs NE alone → NO overall 90-day mortality benefit. Subgroup: less severe septic shock (NE < 15 mcg/min at baseline) showed benefit. Angiotensin II (ATHOS-3): 20–40 ng/kg/min IV — different units from vasopressin, watch for order confusion.

front: The antifungal chart shows azoles inhibit _______, reducing ergosterol synthesis. Fluconazole covers _______ but NOT _______. Voriconazole is first-line for _______ and is monitored by trough level of _______. The azole-fluconazole drug interaction that doubles INR is with _______.
back:
Azoles mechanism: inhibit CYP51 (lanosterol 14α-demethylase) → ↓ ergosterol → fungal membrane disruption
| Fluconazole spectrum: Candida spp. (NOT C. krusei or C. glabrata/parapsilosis — variable MIC)
| Fluconazole: also Cryptococcus neoformans (step-down after AmB induction)
| Voriconazole: first-line for invasive aspergillosis (IDSA 2016)
| Voriconazole trough target: 1–5.5 mcg/mL (trough monitoring reduces toxicity + ensures efficacy)
| Fluconazole + warfarin: INR doubles within 3–5 days — reduce warfarin dose ~50% on initiation
→ CCRN KEY: Which Candida species are resistant to fluconazole:
• C. krusei: intrinsically resistant to fluconazole — always use echinocandin or voriconazole
• C. glabrata: often reduced susceptibility (step-up dosing or switch to echinocandin)
• C. auris (emerging): often pan-resistant; notify infection control; use echinocandin first-line
→ MASTERY NOTE: Voriconazole monitoring parameters:
1. Trough level: 1–5.5 mcg/mL (sub-therapeutic → treatment failure; supra-therapeutic → toxicity)
2. Visual disturbances (photopsia, color changes): common (30%) — transient, dose-related
3. QTc prolongation: baseline ECG + weekly monitoring; avoid with other QTc-prolonging drugs
4. LFTs: monitor q2 weeks; ↑ ALT/AST common; rarely hepatotoxic
5. Photosensitivity + squamous cell skin changes: long-term use in immunocompromised patients.

front: The echinocandin chart shows this class inhibits _______, disrupting the fungal cell wall. The echinocandin requiring NO dose adjustment in renal OR hepatic failure is _______. Echinocandins are NOT active against _______ and _______. The IDSA guideline recommends echinocandins as first-line for candidemia when the patient is _______.
back:
Echinocandins mechanism: inhibit β-1,3-glucan synthase → ↓ cell wall glucan → osmotic lysis
| No dose adjustment needed: anidulafungin (enzymatic degradation in plasma — no organ metabolism)
| Not active against: Cryptococcus neoformans (no glucan in capsule) + Fusarium + Mucorales + Trichosporon
| IDSA: echinocandin first-line for candidemia when: critically ill, prior azole exposure, non-albicans Candida likely
→ CCRN KEY: Echinocandin class advantages in ICU:
• Fungicidal against Candida (azoles are fungistatic) → faster bloodstream clearance
• Excellent Candida biofilm penetration → preferred for catheter-associated candidemia
• Minimal CYP450 drug interactions (not CYP substrates or inhibitors)
• Safe in renal AND hepatic failure — major advantage in critically ill patients
→ MASTERY NOTE: Echinocandin specific differences:
• Micafungin: approved for prophylaxis (50 mg/day) in SCT and for Candida treatment (150 mg/day)
• Caspofungin: reduce to 35 mg/day in severe hepatic failure (Child-Pugh B-C)
• Anidulafungin: loading dose 200 mg × 1, then 100 mg/day; no organ adjustment needed
Step-down to fluconazole from echinocandin when:
• Isolate confirmed susceptible to fluconazole (C. albicans or fluconazole-susceptible C. glabrata)
• Clinical improvement (afebrile, hemodynamically stable, negative blood cultures)
• After minimum 5 days of echinocandin therapy (IDSA guideline)
Duration of candidemia treatment: 14 days from first NEGATIVE blood culture + symptom resolution.

front: The de-escalation chart shows the recommended duration for HAP/VAP is _______ days. Procalcitonin < _______ mcg/mL or ↓ by _______ % from peak is a signal to stop antibiotics. The PRORATA trial showed PCT-guided de-escalation reduced antibiotic exposure from _______ to _______ days without increasing mortality.
back:
HAP/VAP duration: 7 days (IDSA 2016; SHORT trial confirmed non-inferiority of shorter courses)
| PCT-guided stopping threshold: PCT < 0.25 mcg/mL OR ↓ ≥ 80% from peak → consider stopping
| PRORATA trial: PCT-guided vs standard — antibiotic days 14.3 vs 11.6 days (↓ by 2.7 days)
| No increase in mortality or ICU-free days — PCT guidance safe and reduces antibiotic exposure
→ CCRN KEY: De-escalation principles in ICU:
• 48–72h review: assess cultures, clinical response, organ function — de-escalate if improving
• Never de-escalate: S. aureus bacteremia, Candida, Aspergillosis without minimum treatment
• CAP duration: 5 days (IDSA 2019 update) if afebrile × 48h, hemodynamically stable
• S. aureus bacteremia: minimum 14 days from first negative blood culture (28 days if complicated/endocarditis)
→ MASTERY NOTE: Antibiotic duration by source:
• Uncomplicated UTI (CAUTI): 7 days if respond; catheter removal shortens duration needed
• Intra-abdominal infection (post-source control): 4 days adequate (STOP-IT trial, NEJM 2015)
• Skin/soft tissue (cellulitis): 5 days if improved (step-down oral as soon as able)
• Clostridium difficile (non-severe): fidaxomicin 200 mg BID × 10d OR vancomycin 125 mg QID × 10d
Broad antibiotic exposure consequence: C. diff, antibiotic-resistant organism selection, microbiome disruption — every unnecessary day of antibiotics has measurable adverse effects.

front: On the specific shock types chart, the FIRST treatment for anaphylaxis is _______ given _______ (site and route), not IV antihistamines. Neurogenic shock from spinal cord injury differs from other shock types because the heart rate is _______ (not elevated). The MAP target in acute spinal cord injury is ≥ _______ mmHg to maintain cord perfusion.
back:
Anaphylaxis first treatment: epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg IM (anterolateral thigh)
| IM preferred over IV for non-arrest anaphylaxis (faster peak concentration than IV in this setting)
| Do NOT delay epi for IV access: mortality from anaphylaxis = delayed epinephrine
| Diphenhydramine + steroids: adjuncts only — they do NOT reverse circulatory collapse
| Neurogenic shock: ↓ HR (bradycardia from loss of cardiac sympathetic fibers) + ↓ BP
| Distinguishing feature: shock with BRADYCARDIA (not tachycardia as in other shock types)
| MAP target in SCI: ≥ 85–90 mmHg for 5–7 days (spinal cord perfusion pressure maintenance)
→ CCRN KEY: Neurogenic shock vasopressor selection:
• Phenylephrine (pure α1): for hypotension WITHOUT bradycardia — avoids reflex tachycardia
• Norepinephrine (α1 + β1): useful when bradycardia + hypotension coexist
• Dopamine: β1 + α1 — can use when bradycardia limits phenylephrine choice
• Atropine: for symptomatic bradycardia in spinal shock
→ MASTERY NOTE: Obstructive shock management:
• Massive PE: IVF 500 mL bolus (↑ RV preload) + NE (maintains coronary perfusion) → thrombolysis or thrombectomy
• Cardiac tamponade: maintain HR (NE/dopamine) + preload (IVF) + heart rate to compensate fixed stroke volume
  Pericardiocentesis: definitive; ultrasound-guided
  Avoid: PEEP (↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → cardiac arrest)
• Tension pneumothorax: needle decompression (2nd ICS MCL) → tube thoracostomy — vasopressors temporize.

front: The beta-blocker chart shows carvedilol has _______ receptor blocking activity. The MERIT-HF trial showed metoprolol _______ XL reduced mortality in HFrEF by _______%. In thyroid storm, propranolol is preferred over cardioselective beta-blockers because it also inhibits _______ conversion.
back:
Carvedilol receptor blocking activity: β1 + β2 + α1 (non-selective beta + alpha-1)
| Additional α1 block: ↓ afterload + antioxidant properties beyond pure beta-blockade
| MERIT-HF trial: metoprolol succinate (XL) vs placebo in HFrEF (EF < 40%)
| Result: 34% relative risk reduction in all-cause mortality (34% RRR); also ↓ sudden cardiac death
| Propranolol in thyroid storm: blocks T4 → T3 peripheral conversion (in addition to β-blockade)
| Selective agents (metoprolol): only block β-receptors — do NOT inhibit T4→T3 conversion
→ CCRN KEY: Beta-blockers with mortality benefit in HFrEF (class effect only for 3 agents):
• Carvedilol (COPERNICUS trial)
• Metoprolol succinate XL (MERIT-HF trial)
• Bisoprolol (CIBIS-II trial)
• NOT extended to all beta-blockers — class effect is NOT proven for all
• Atenolol, propranolol: no mortality benefit in HFrEF — do NOT substitute
→ MASTERY NOTE: Beta-blocker in ACUTE decompensated HF:
• Do NOT start new beta-blocker in acute decompensated HF with cardiogenic shock
• Continue home beta-blocker if hemodynamically stable (stopping worsens outcomes)
• If hemodynamically unstable: reduce or hold dose temporarily; restart when euvolemic and stable
Carvedilol start: 3.125 mg PO BID with food; double every 2 weeks as tolerated to max 25 mg BID.

front: On the acute decompensated HF chart, the DOSE trial showed the high-dose furosemide strategy results in _______ without increasing _______.
back: greater diuresis and symptom relief (better decongestion) → without increasing rates of worsening renal function compared to low-dose strategy

front: The nephrotoxicity monitoring chart shows aminoglycoside AKI is triggered when SCr rises _______, with the key prevention strategy being _______.
back: SCr ↑ 0.3 mg/dL over 48h or >1.5× baseline → extended-interval dosing (EID) 5–7 mg/kg q24h: maximizes Cmax/MIC and minimizes nephrotoxicity vs multiple daily dosing

front: The RASS targets chart shows general ICU ventilated patients target RASS _______, while patients on NMBAs require RASS _______ with mandatory _______ monitoring.
back: RASS 0 to −1 (light sedation — awake/arousable, PADIS 2018 guideline) → RASS −4 to −5 for NMBAs → BIS 40–60 or TOF monitoring mandatory (patient could be awake without movement)

front: The SAT/SBT chart shows a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) passes when RSBI is _______, where RSBI is calculated as _______.
back: RSBI <105 breaths/min/L (predicts successful extubation) → RSBI = respiratory rate ÷ tidal volume in liters (RR/Vt); >105 = high extubation failure risk

front: The warfarin INR targets chart shows mechanical mitral valve requires INR _______, and major bleeding with warfarin is reversed using _______ as first-line agent.
back: INR 2.5–3.5 (higher thrombotic risk vs aortic valve) → 4F-PCC (Kcentra) 25–50 units/kg + Vit K 10 mg IV slow infusion — onset 15 min vs 6–12h+ for FFP

front: On the argatroban monitoring chart, hepatic failure patients require a starting dose of _______ with aPTT target _______, lower than the standard goal.
back: 0.5 mcg/kg/min (25% of standard 2 mcg/kg/min) → aPTT target 1.5–2× baseline (vs 1.5–3× standard) — argatroban is hepatically cleared; ↑ drug effect in liver failure
